concepts.def: A property of matter that gives rise to electric forces. There are two types, positive and negative: like charges repel and unlike charges attract, and the forces the two charges exert on each other are equal in size and opposite in direction (Newton's third law). A charged object also attracts an uncharged one, by inducing charge separation in it. SI unit: coulomb (C).

The electric force between two point charges q₁ and q₂ a distance r apart is F = k q₁q₂/r², directed along the line joining them: repulsive for like charges, attractive for unlike charges. For charged spheres with a uniform (spherically symmetric) charge distribution, r is measured between their centres.

concepts.term: Coulomb constant and permittivity of free space
concepts.def: k = 1/4πε₀, where ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹ (C² N⁻¹ m⁻²) is the permittivity of free space; k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². These values apply to charges in a vacuum (and very nearly in air).

When the charges are in a medium, ε₀ is replaced by the permittivity ε of that medium: F = q₁q₂/4πεr². Insulating media have ε > ε₀ (for example ε ≈ 80ε₀ for water), so the force between the same charges at the same separation is smaller than in a vacuum. SI unit: F m⁻¹.

A charged body whose size is negligible compared with the distances involved, so that all its charge can be taken to be at one point. A sphere with a uniform charge distribution behaves, at points outside it, as a point charge at its centre.

The total electric charge of an isolated system is constant. Charge is never created or destroyed: charging an object moves existing charge (in solids, electrons) from one body to another, so one body gains exactly the charge the other loses.

concepts.term: Quantization of charge and the elementary charge
concepts.def: Electric charge exists only in whole-number multiples of the elementary charge e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the size of the charge on an electron or a proton: q = ne, where n is an integer.

Charged oil drops are observed between two horizontal parallel plates. Adjusting the potential difference until a drop is held stationary gives qE = mg, so q = mgd/V for a drop of known weight. Millikan found that every drop's charge was a whole-number multiple of one smallest value, about 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C: evidence that charge is quantized.

In a metal (a conductor) some electrons are free to move through the material, so charge spreads over it and can flow to or from it. In an insulator the electrons are bound to their atoms, so charge placed on it stays where it was put, although the molecules can still be polarized.

When two different insulators are rubbed together, electrons are transferred from one surface to the other. The body that gains electrons becomes negatively charged; the other is left with an equal positive charge.

When a charged conductor touches another conductor, charge flows between them until there is no potential difference between them. For two identical conducting spheres the total charge is shared equally.

A charged object brought near a conductor, without touching it, causes the conductor's free electrons to redistribute: charge opposite in sign to the inducing charge gathers on the near side and like charge on the far side. No charge passes between the two objects.

Connecting a conductor to the Earth, a very large reservoir of charge. Electrons can then flow between the conductor and the Earth. If the conductor is earthed while a charged object is held nearby and the earth connection is broken before the object is removed, the conductor is left with a charge opposite in sign to that of the object (charging by induction).

The electric force per unit charge experienced by a small positive test charge placed at a point: E = F/q. It is a vector in the direction of the force on a positive charge; a negative charge experiences a force opposite to E. E at a point does not depend on the test charge used. SI unit: N C⁻¹ (equivalent to V m⁻¹).

concepts.term: Radial field of a point charge or charged sphere
concepts.def: Combining E = F/q with Coulomb's law gives E = kQ/r² at a distance r from a point charge Q, directed away from a positive charge and towards a negative one. Outside a charged conducting sphere the field is the same as that of a point charge at its centre; inside the conductor the electric field is zero.

A line drawn so that its direction at every point is the direction of the electric field (the force on a positive test charge). Electric field lines start on positive charges and end on negative charges (or at infinity), never cross, and meet the surface of a conductor at right angles.

A point at which the resultant electric field of two or more charges is zero. For two equal like charges it is at the midpoint between them; for unequal like charges it is closer to the smaller charge. No neutral point exists between two unlike charges.

The number of field lines crossing unit area at right angles to the field. The field strength is proportional to this density: the field is strongest where the lines are closest together. For a point charge the same number of lines crosses every sphere of area 4πr², so the density, and E, falls as 1/r².

Between two oppositely charged parallel plates, away from their edges, the field has the same magnitude and direction at every point: E = V/d, where V is the potential difference between the plates and d their separation. The field lines are parallel, equally spaced and run from the positive to the negative plate. SI unit: V m⁻¹.
Near the edges of a pair of parallel plates the field is not uniform: the field lines bulge outwards beyond the edges of the plates, so E = V/d applies only in the central region.

A line whose direction at every point is the direction in which the north pole of a small compass would point. Magnetic field lines form closed loops (outside a magnet they run from its north pole to its south pole, and inside it from south to north), never cross, and are closest together where the field is strongest.

For a straight current-carrying wire: grip the wire with the right hand, thumb in the direction of the conventional current; the fingers curl in the direction of the magnetic field lines, which are concentric circles centred on the wire. For a coil or solenoid, fingers curled in the direction of the current give the thumb pointing along the field inside it (towards the north-pole end).

concepts.term: Magnetic field of a coil and of a solenoid
concepts.def: At the centre of a flat circular coil the field is along the coil's axis, perpendicular to its plane. Inside a long air-core solenoid the field lines are parallel and evenly spaced along the axis (a strong, nearly uniform field); outside, the pattern is like that of a bar magnet, with the lines forming closed loops through the inside.

The electric potential energy E_p of a system of charges is the work done to assemble the system from infinite separation of its components (where E_p = 0). It belongs to the system, not to any one charge. It is positive for like charges (work must be done to push them together) and negative for unlike charges. SI unit: joule (J).

concepts.term: Electric potential energy of two point charges
concepts.def: For two point charges q₁ and q₂ a distance r apart, E_p = k q₁q₂/r, with the signs of the charges included. E_p varies as 1/r, not 1/r², and is a scalar.

Electric potential is a scalar, defined as zero at infinity. The potential at a point due to several charges is the algebraic sum of the potentials due to each charge, V = Σ kQᵢ/rᵢ, with the sign of each charge included and no directions involved.

The electric potential V_e at a point is the work done per unit charge to bring a small positive test charge from infinity to that point. For a point charge Q, V_e = kQ/r: positive near a positive charge, negative near a negative charge. SI unit: volt (V = J C⁻¹).

The electric field strength equals minus the potential gradient: E = −ΔV_e/Δr. The field points in the direction in which the potential decreases most rapidly, and its magnitude is the rate of change of potential with distance. In a uniform field the potential changes linearly with distance along the field.

The work done by an external force in moving a charge q between two points at constant kinetic energy is W = qΔV_e, where ΔV_e is the change in potential. It depends only on the start and end points, not on the path taken. The work done by the field is −qΔV_e.

The energy transferred when a charge of e moves through a potential difference of 1 V: 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. A particle of charge q = ne moving through a potential difference ΔV has work done on it of n × ΔV electronvolts.

A surface on which every point is at the same electric potential. Around a point charge they are concentric spheres, closer together near the charge for equal steps of potential; between parallel plates they are equally spaced planes parallel to the plates; the whole of a charged conductor (solid or hollow), including the space inside a hollow one, is at a single potential equal to that at its surface. Around a collection of point charges, the equipotentials close to each charge are nearly spherical surfaces around that charge; further out they merge into surfaces that enclose several charges, and far away they approach spheres around the whole collection. Outside a charged conducting sphere, solid or hollow, they are concentric spheres, as for a point charge at its centre.

Field lines cross equipotential surfaces at right angles and point from higher to lower potential. Because the field is perpendicular to an equipotential, no work is done in moving a charge along one. Where equipotentials (at equal potential steps) are closer together, the field is stronger.

mcqs.q: Which statement about electric charges and the forces they exert is correct?
options: Unlike charges attract each other, but the larger charge exerts the larger force.
Unlike charges attract, and the two forces on them are equal in size.
A charged object exerts no force at all on any uncharged object near it.
A stationary positive charge attracts a magnet's north pole and repels its south pole.
mcqs.specStatementText: the direction of forces between the two types of electric charge
mcqs.explain: Two types of charge: like repel, unlike attract. The force of each charge on the other forms a Newton's third law pair, so the forces are equal in size and opposite in direction, whatever the sizes of the charges.
rationales: A student who thinks the 'stronger' charge pulls harder picks this. F = kq₁q₂/r² depends on the product of the charges, which is the same for both; by Newton's third law the forces are equal and opposite.

Two types of charge: like repel, unlike attract. The force of each charge on the other forms a Newton's third law pair, so the forces are equal in size and opposite in direction, whatever the sizes of the charges.

A student who thinks attraction needs two opposite charges picks this. A charged object induces charge separation in a nearby uncharged object; the nearer, opposite charge is attracted more strongly than the further one is repelled, so there is a net attraction.

A student who treats charges and magnetic poles as the same kind of thing picks this. A stationary charge exerts no magnetic force on either pole; magnetic forces act on moving charges and currents. Any small attraction of the magnet is by induction and acts on both ends alike.

mcqs.q: Two small spheres, treated as point charges, carry charges of +4.0 nC and +6.0 nC. They are 2.0 cm apart, immersed in an oil of permittivity ε = 4.2 × 10⁻¹¹ F m⁻¹. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹. What is the magnitude of the electric force between them?
mcqs.specStatementText: Coulomb’s law as given by F = k q₁q₂/r² for charged bodies treated as point charges where k = 1/4πε₀
mcqs.working: In the oil, F = q₁q₂/(4πεr²) with ε = 4.2 × 10⁻¹¹ F m⁻¹ and r = 2.0 cm = 0.020 m. F = (4.0 × 10⁻⁹ C)(6.0 × 10⁻⁹ C)/(4π × 4.2 × 10⁻¹¹ F m⁻¹ × (0.020 m)²) = 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁷/2.11 × 10⁻¹³ = 1.1 × 10⁻⁴ N (repulsive). For comparison, in a vacuum (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹) the force would be 5.4 × 10⁻⁴ N.
rationales: A student who uses the vacuum value ε₀ (k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²) whatever the medium gets 5.4 × 10⁻⁴ N, the force in a vacuum. In the oil ε is 4.7 times larger, so the force is 4.7 times smaller.

A student who thinks a higher permittivity 'permits' a larger force multiplies the vacuum force by ε/ε₀ = 4.75 and gets 2.6 × 10⁻³ N. Permittivity is in the denominator of Coulomb's law: the force is divided by 4.75, not multiplied.
A student who writes k = 1/ε, dropping the 4π, gets q₁q₂/εr² = 1.4 × 10⁻³ N. The Coulomb constant in a medium is k = 1/4πε, so this answer is 4π times too large.

mcqs.q: Two small insulating spheres, each of diameter 2.0 cm, carry charges of +10 nC and +15 nC spread uniformly over them. They are in a vacuum with a gap of 3.0 cm between their surfaces. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the magnitude of the electric force between them?
mcqs.specStatementText: Coulomb’s law as given by F = k q₁q₂/r² for charged bodies treated as point charges where k = 1/4πε₀
mcqs.explain: Each uniformly charged sphere acts as a point charge at its centre, so r = 1.0 cm + 3.0 cm + 1.0 cm = 5.0 cm = 0.050 m. F = kq₁q₂/r² = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 10 × 10⁻⁹ × 15 × 10⁻⁹/(0.050)² = 5.4 × 10⁻⁴ N.
mcqs.working: Uniformly charged spheres act as point charges at their centres: r = gap + two radii = 3.0 cm + 1.0 cm + 1.0 cm = 5.0 cm = 0.050 m. F = kq₁q₂/r² = (8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)(10 × 10⁻⁹ C)(15 × 10⁻⁹ C)/(0.050 m)² = 1.349 × 10⁻⁶/2.5 × 10⁻³ = 5.4 × 10⁻⁴ N (repulsive).
rationales: Each uniformly charged sphere acts as a point charge at its centre, so r = 1.0 cm + 3.0 cm + 1.0 cm = 5.0 cm = 0.050 m. F = kq₁q₂/r² = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 10 × 10⁻⁹ × 15 × 10⁻⁹/(0.050)² = 5.4 × 10⁻⁴ N.
A student who uses the gap between the surfaces, 0.030 m, as r gets 1.5 × 10⁻³ N. The charges act as if at the centres, which are 0.050 m apart.
A student who adds the full diameters to the gap, r = 2.0 + 3.0 + 2.0 = 7.0 cm, gets 2.8 × 10⁻⁴ N. From each surface to its centre is the radius, 1.0 cm, not the diameter.
A student who divides by r instead of r² gets kq₁q₂/r = 2.70 × 10⁻⁵ (which is not even in newtons). Coulomb's law is an inverse-square law: divide by (0.050 m)².

mcqs.q: Two identical small metal spheres, X and Y, stand on insulating bases. X carries a charge of +5.0 nC and Y carries −3.0 nC. The spheres are touched together and then separated. What is the charge on X after they are separated?
options: 4.0 nC
0.0 nC
5.0 nC
1.0 nC
mcqs.specStatementText: the conservation of electric charge
mcqs.explain: Charge is conserved: the total is +5.0 nC + (−3.0 nC) = +2.0 nC. Electrons flow between the touching conductors until the identical spheres share this equally, so X is left with +1.0 nC (and Y with +1.0 nC).
mcqs.working: Total charge before = +5.0 nC + (−3.0 nC) = +2.0 nC. Charge is conserved, and identical conducting spheres share it equally on contact: each is left with +2.0 nC/2 = +1.0 nC. (4.0 nC of electrons, i.e. 2.5 × 10¹⁰ electrons, flow from Y to X.)
rationales: A student who adds the sizes of the charges without their signs gets 8.0 nC in total and 4.0 nC each. Charge is signed: −3.0 nC cancels 3.0 nC of the +5.0 nC, leaving +2.0 nC to share.

A student who thinks opposite charges neutralize each other completely picks this. Only 3.0 nC of each sign can cancel; the remaining +2.0 nC is conserved and shared, so neither sphere is left uncharged.
A student who thinks static charge stays where it was put picks this. The spheres are metal: free electrons flow from Y to X when they touch, until the charge is shared equally.

Charge is conserved: the total is +5.0 nC + (−3.0 nC) = +2.0 nC. Electrons flow between the touching conductors until the identical spheres share this equally, so X is left with +1.0 nC (and Y with +1.0 nC).

mcqs.q: In an experiment of Millikan's type, the charges on four oil drops were measured in arbitrary units as 7.50, 12.5, 17.5 and 22.5 units. Assuming that electric charge is quantized, what is the largest value of the basic unit of charge that is consistent with all four results?
options: 7.50 units
2.50 units
15.0 units
5.00 units
mcqs.specStatementText: Millikan’s experiment as evidence for quantization of electric charge
mcqs.explain: The basic unit must divide every charge a whole number of times. 7.50, 12.5, 17.5 and 22.5 are 3, 5, 7 and 9 times 2.50, and no larger value divides all four: 5.00 fails for 7.50 (1.5 units) and 7.50 fails for 12.5.
mcqs.working: Test candidate units by dividing each charge by them. Unit 2.50: 7.50/2.50 = 3, 12.5/2.50 = 5, 17.5/2.50 = 7, 22.5/2.50 = 9, all whole numbers. Unit 5.00: 7.50/5.00 = 1.5, not whole. Unit 7.50: 12.5/7.50 = 1.67, not whole. The largest consistent unit is 2.50 units.
rationales: A student who takes the smallest measured charge as the unit picks this. 12.5 units is 1.67 times 7.50 units, not a whole number, so the smallest drop must itself carry several units.

The basic unit must divide every charge a whole number of times. 7.50, 12.5, 17.5 and 22.5 are 3, 5, 7 and 9 times 2.50, and no larger value divides all four: 5.00 fails for 7.50 (1.5 units) and 7.50 fails for 12.5.
A student who averages the four charges gets 15.0 units. The drops carry different numbers of units, so their mean is not a unit of charge; 7.50 units is less than it, which a unit could not allow.

A student who takes the constant step between the sorted values as the unit gets 5.00 units. But 7.50 units is 1.5 times 5.00 units, so 5.00 cannot be the unit; every charge must be a whole-number multiple.

mcqs.q: A polythene rod becomes negatively charged when it is rubbed with a woollen cloth. Which statement explains how the rod becomes charged?
options: Rubbing creates new negative charge in the surface layer of the rod.
Protons move from the rod to the cloth, leaving the rod with a negative charge.
Electrons move from the cloth to the rod, so the rod gains extra electrons.
Electrons move from the rod to the cloth, as negative means a lack of electrons.
mcqs.specStatementText: that the electric charge can be transferred between bodies using friction, electrostatic induction and by contact, including the role of grounding (earthing)
mcqs.explain: Rubbing transfers electrons between the surfaces. The rod gains electrons (an excess makes it negative) and the cloth loses the same number, becoming equally positive: charge is conserved.
rationales: A student who thinks friction generates charge, as it generates heat, picks this. Charge is never created: the cloth ends up with a positive charge exactly equal in size to the rod's negative charge.
A student who thinks positive charges move during charging picks this. In a solid the protons are locked in the nuclei; only electrons are transferred.
Rubbing transfers electrons between the surfaces. The rod gains electrons (an excess makes it negative) and the cloth loses the same number, becoming equally positive: charge is conserved.
A student who reads 'negative' as 'a shortage' picks this. Electrons carry negative charge, so a negative rod has more electrons than normal: they moved onto it, not off it.

mcqs.q: An uncharged metal sphere stands on an insulating base. A negatively charged rod is held near the sphere, without touching it. While the rod is held there, the sphere is connected to earth by a wire. The wire is then removed, and after that the rod is taken away. Which statement describes the electron flow in the wire and the final charge on the sphere?
options: Electrons flowed from the sphere to earth, and the sphere is left positively charged.
Electrons flowed from earth to the sphere, and it is left negatively charged.
Electrons flowed from the sphere to earth, and the sphere is left with no charge.
Electrons crossed from the rod to the sphere, and the sphere is left negatively charged.
mcqs.specStatementText: that the electric charge can be transferred between bodies using friction, electrostatic induction and by contact, including the role of grounding (earthing)
mcqs.explain: The negative rod repels free electrons in the sphere; with the earth wire connected they flow away to earth. Breaking the connection before removing the rod traps the deficit, so the sphere is left positive (charging by induction).
rationales: The negative rod repels free electrons in the sphere; with the earth wire connected they flow away to earth. Breaking the connection before removing the rod traps the deficit, so the sphere is left positive (charging by induction).
A student who thinks the Earth always supplies electrons picks this. The nearby negative rod repels electrons, so they are pushed out of the sphere into the earth, not drawn in.

A student who thinks earthing always leaves an object uncharged picks this. Electrons left the sphere and could not return once the wire was removed; by conservation of charge the sphere must now be positive.
A student who thinks induction transfers charge from the rod picks this. The rod never touches the sphere and no charge crosses the gap; induction only redistributes the sphere's own electrons.

mcqs.q: Which statement defines the electric field strength at a point?
options: The force on any charged object that is placed at that point, measured in newtons.
The force per unit charge on any small charge, in the direction of the force on it.
The energy per unit charge transferred to a small charge placed at that point.
The force per unit charge exerted on a small positive test charge placed at that point.
mcqs.specStatementText: the electric field strength as given by E = F/q
mcqs.explain: E = F/q, defined using a small positive test charge, so that the test charge does not disturb the source charges and the direction of E is the direction of the force on a positive charge. Unit: N C⁻¹.
rationales: A student who equates field strength with the force picks this. The force depends on the charge placed there; the field strength is the force per unit charge, which does not.

A student who thinks the field points along the force on any charge picks this. For a negative charge the force is opposite to the field; the field direction is defined by the force on a positive charge.
A student who confuses field strength with potential difference picks this. Energy per unit charge is measured in volts; field strength is force per unit charge, in N C⁻¹.

E = F/q, defined using a small positive test charge, so that the test charge does not disturb the source charges and the direction of E is the direction of the force on a positive charge. Unit: N C⁻¹.

mcqs.q: At point P, a charge of +2.0 µC experiences an electric force of 5.0 × 10⁻³ N directed east. This charge is removed and a charge of −6.0 µC is placed at P; the charges that produce the field do not move. Taking east as positive, what is the electric force on the −6.0 µC charge?
mcqs.specStatementText: the electric field strength as given by E = F/q
mcqs.explain: E at P = F/q = 5.0 × 10⁻³ N/2.0 × 10⁻⁶ C = 2.5 × 10³ N C⁻¹ east, and it does not change when the test charge is replaced. F = qE = (−6.0 × 10⁻⁶)(+2.5 × 10³) = −1.5 × 10⁻² N, i.e. 1.5 × 10⁻² N west.
mcqs.working: E = F/q = (5.0 × 10⁻³ N)/(2.0 × 10⁻⁶ C) = 2.5 × 10³ N C⁻¹, directed east (the direction of the force on the positive charge). E at P is unchanged when the test charge is replaced. F = qE = (−6.0 × 10⁻⁶ C)(+2.5 × 10³ N C⁻¹) = −1.5 × 10⁻² N: 1.5 × 10⁻² N directed west.
rationales: A student who thinks every charge is pushed along the field picks this. The field is east, but the charge is negative, so F = qE points west: the sign is negative.

A student who thinks the force at a point is fixed reverses its direction for the negative charge but keeps its size. The field is fixed; the force is proportional to the charge, so it is three times larger.
E at P = F/q = 5.0 × 10⁻³ N/2.0 × 10⁻⁶ C = 2.5 × 10³ N C⁻¹ east, and it does not change when the test charge is replaced. F = qE = (−6.0 × 10⁻⁶)(+2.5 × 10³) = −1.5 × 10⁻² N, i.e. 1.5 × 10⁻² N west.

A student who treats the field strength as the force takes E = 5.0 × 10⁻³ (the force on the first charge) and then uses F = qE = (−6.0 × 10⁻⁶)(5.0 × 10⁻³) = −3.0 × 10⁻⁸ N. The field strength is force per unit charge: E = 5.0 × 10⁻³ N/2.0 × 10⁻⁶ C = 2.5 × 10³ N C⁻¹.

mcqs.q: Two point charges of +4.0 nC and +1.0 nC are fixed 0.30 m apart. At one point on the line between them the resultant electric field strength is zero. How far is this point from the +4.0 nC charge?
mcqs.specStatementText: the electric field strength as given by E = F/q
mcqs.explain: At the neutral point the two fields are equal and opposite: k(4.0 nC)/x² = k(1.0 nC)/(0.30 − x)². Taking square roots, x/(0.30 − x) = 2, so x = 0.20 m from the +4.0 nC charge (0.10 m from the +1.0 nC charge).
mcqs.working: Between two like charges the fields are opposite in direction, so E = 0 where kQ₁/x² = kQ₂/(d − x)². With Q₁ = 4.0 nC, Q₂ = 1.0 nC and d = 0.30 m: x/(0.30 m − x) = √(Q₁/Q₂) = √4 = 2 ⇒ x = 2(0.30 m − x) ⇒ 3x = 0.60 m ⇒ x = 0.20 m from the +4.0 nC charge.
rationales: A student who puts the neutral point of any two like charges at the midpoint picks this. At 0.15 m the +4.0 nC charge's field is four times the other's; the fields balance only nearer the smaller charge.
A student who takes the fields as proportional to 1/r solves 4/x = 1/(0.30 − x) and gets 0.24 m. The fields vary as 1/r², so the distance ratio is √4 = 2, not 4.

A student who treats the neutral point like a centre of mass, nearer the larger charge, divides 0.30 m in the ratio 1 : 4 from the +4.0 nC charge. The larger charge's field is stronger, so the balance point must be further from it, not nearer.

At the neutral point the two fields are equal and opposite: k(4.0 nC)/x² = k(1.0 nC)/(0.30 − x)². Taking square roots, x/(0.30 − x) = 2, so x = 0.20 m from the +4.0 nC charge (0.10 m from the +1.0 nC charge).

mcqs.q: A student sketches the electric field lines around two equal positive point charges a short distance apart. Which description of a correct sketch is right?
options: Lines leave each charge and curve away from the other, with a neutral point at the midpoint.
Lines leave each charge, and some of them cross one another in the region midway between them.
Lines run from one charge to the other, joining the two charges across the gap.
Straight radial lines leave each charge, exactly as if the other charge were absent.
mcqs.specStatementText: electric field lines
mcqs.explain: Like charges: every line starts on a positive charge and goes out to infinity. Lines between the charges curve away from the other charge, and the midpoint is a neutral point where the two fields cancel (E = 0), so no line crosses it.
rationales: Like charges: every line starts on a positive charge and goes out to infinity. Lines between the charges curve away from the other charge, and the midpoint is a neutral point where the two fields cancel (E = 0), so no line crosses it.
A student who overlays each charge's field picks this. The resultant field has one direction at each point, so field lines can never cross.
A student who generalizes the pattern for opposite charges picks this. Lines end only on negative charges; with two positive charges no line can end on the other charge.
A student who does not add the two fields picks this. At each point the field is the vector sum of both, so the lines near the charges are curved, not straight and radial.

mcqs.q: A hollow metal sphere on an insulating stand is given a positive charge. Which description of the electric field lines is correct?
options: Lines inside as well as outside, since the charge is spread through the whole sphere.
None inside; outside, radial lines pointing away, as if from a point charge at the centre.
Lines leave the surface both ways, pointing inwards and outwards from the charge.
None inside; outside, parallel and equally spaced lines, as the charge is spread evenly.
mcqs.specStatementText: electric field lines
mcqs.explain: The charge sits on the outer surface of the conductor and the field inside is zero. Outside, the field is that of a point charge at the centre: radial lines leaving the surface at right angles, spreading out with distance.
rationales: A student who pictures the charge spread through the sphere picks this. In a conductor the charge moves to the outer surface until the field inside is zero.

The charge sits on the outer surface of the conductor and the field inside is zero. Outside, the field is that of a point charge at the centre: radial lines leaving the surface at right angles, spreading out with distance.
A student who treats each bit of surface charge as an isolated point charge picks this. Inside, the fields of all the surface charges cancel exactly, so no lines point inwards.
A student who links an evenly spread charge with a uniform field picks this. Outside a sphere the lines are radial and spread out, so the field weakens as 1/r²; parallel lines belong to flat plates.

mcqs.q: Which description of the electric field lines of two oppositely charged parallel plates is correct?
options: Parallel and evenly spaced from the positive to the negative plate, stopping sharply at the plate edges.
From the positive to the negative plate, closest near each plate and widest apart midway.
Closed loops that leave the positive plate and curve round to return to it, as magnetic field lines do.
Parallel and evenly spaced from the positive to the negative plate, bulging outwards at the edges.
mcqs.specStatementText: electric field lines
mcqs.explain: In the central region the field is uniform: parallel, equally spaced lines from + to −. Near the edges the lines curve outwards beyond the plates (the edge effect), so the field there is not uniform.
rationales: A student who ignores edge effects picks this. The lines cannot simply stop at the edges: they curve outwards there, and the field is non-uniform near the edges.
A student who applies point-charge thinking to the plates picks this. Away from the edges the field between large plates is uniform: the lines are equally spaced right across the gap.
A student who carries over the closed loops of magnetic fields picks this. Electric field lines start on positive charge and end on negative charge; they do not return to where they began.
In the central region the field is uniform: parallel, equally spaced lines from + to −. Near the edges the lines curve outwards beyond the plates (the edge effect), so the field there is not uniform.

mcqs.q: The field lines of an isolated negative point charge spread out in three dimensions, and the same number of lines passes through every sphere centred on the charge. Point P is 2.0 cm from the charge and point Q is 6.0 cm from it. How does the electric field strength at P compare with that at Q?
options: E at P is 3 times E at Q, as P is 3 times closer, so the lines are 3 times as close.
E is the same at P and Q, as each line that passes P's sphere also passes Q's sphere.
E at P is 9 times E at Q, as there are 9 times as many lines per unit area at P.
E cannot be compared, as the number of field lines drawn is merely an arbitrary choice.
mcqs.specStatementText: the relationship between field line density and field strength
mcqs.explain: The same lines pass through spheres of area 4πr². Q's sphere has 3² = 9 times the area of P's, so the line density, and hence E, is 9 times greater at P, in agreement with E = kQ/r².
mcqs.working: The same number N of lines crosses spheres of area 4πr². Density at P ∝ N/(4π × 2.0²), at Q ∝ N/(4π × 6.0²). Ratio P : Q = 6.0²/2.0² = 9. Since E ∝ line density, E_P = 9E_Q, consistent with E = kQ/r².
rationales: A student who reads spacing from a flat sketch, or assumes E ∝ 1/r, picks this. In three dimensions the lines spread over an area ∝ r², so the density changes by 3² = 9.
A student who thinks a field line carries the same strength along its length picks this. The same lines spread over a larger area further out, so they are less dense and the field is weaker at Q.
The same lines pass through spheres of area 4πr². Q's sphere has 3² = 9 times the area of P's, so the line density, and hence E, is 9 times greater at P, in agreement with E = kQ/r².
A student who thinks line density is a mere drawing convention picks this. Whatever number is chosen, it is fixed within the picture, so the relative density at P and Q compares the field strengths.

mcqs.q: Two parallel metal plates 5.0 mm apart in a vacuum are connected to a 1500 V supply. An electron is between the plates, well away from their edges. Take e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the magnitude of the electric force on the electron?
mcqs.specStatementText: the uniform electric field strength between parallel plates as given by E = V/d
mcqs.working: E = V/d = 1500 V/(5.0 × 10⁻³ m) = 3.0 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹, uniform between the plates away from the edges. F = eE = (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)(3.0 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹) = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁴ N, directed towards the positive plate.
rationales: A student who substitutes d = 5.0 without converting millimetres to metres gets E = 300 V m⁻¹ and F = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁷ N. d must be 5.0 × 10⁻³ m.
A student who multiplies V by d gets E = 7.5 and F = 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ N. The field is the potential difference per unit distance, E = V/d, in V m⁻¹.
A student who uses F = qV gets 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁶, but qV is the energy (in J) an electron gains crossing the gap, not the force on it. F = qE = qV/d.

mcqs.q: Two parallel plates remain connected to the same supply while their separation is doubled. A small charged dust particle is held between the plates, well away from their edges. How does the electric force on the particle change?
options: It is unchanged, since E depends only on V, which the supply fixes.
It halves, since E = V/d and d has doubled while V is unchanged.
It falls to a quarter, since E ∝ 1/d², like the field of a point charge.
It doubles, since E = Vd and d has doubled at constant V.
mcqs.specStatementText: the uniform electric field strength between parallel plates as given by E = V/d
mcqs.explain: The supply keeps V fixed. Between the plates E = V/d, so doubling d halves E, and F = qE halves.
rationales: A student who thinks the field is set by the potential difference alone picks this. E = V/d: the same potential difference across twice the separation gives half the field, so E and F halve.
The supply keeps V fixed. Between the plates E = V/d, so doubling d halves E, and F = qE halves.
A student who applies the inverse-square law to every field picks this. Only radial fields fall as 1/r²; between plates E = V/d, so doubling d halves E.
A student who multiplies V by d picks this. E = V/d (volts per metre): a wider gap at the same potential difference gives a weaker field.

mcqs.q: A long, straight, vertical wire carries a steady current upwards. Point P is 5.0 cm due east of the wire, level with it. What is the direction of the magnetic field of the wire at P?
options: Due south, at a tangent to a circle around the wire
Due east, directly away from the wire along a radius
Due north, at a tangent to a circle centred on the wire
Vertically upwards, parallel to the direction of the current
mcqs.specStatementText: magnetic field lines.
mcqs.explain: Right-hand grip rule: thumb upwards along the current, fingers curl anticlockwise when seen from above. The field lines are circles round the wire; at a point east of the wire, anticlockwise means due north.
rationales: A student who uses the left hand, or curls the fingers the wrong way, gets the reversed direction. With the right thumb upwards the field circulates anticlockwise seen from above, which is north at P.

A student who expects a radial pattern, like the electric field of a charged wire, picks this. The magnetic field lines of a straight wire are circles around it, so the field at P is tangential, not radial.

Right-hand grip rule: thumb upwards along the current, fingers curl anticlockwise when seen from above. The field lines are circles round the wire; at a point east of the wire, anticlockwise means due north.
A student who thinks the field points along the current picks this. The field of a straight current circulates around the wire, perpendicular to it.

mcqs.q: A flat horizontal circular coil carries a steady current that flows anticlockwise when viewed from above. What is the direction of the magnetic field at the centre of the coil?
options: There is no field: the fields of opposite sides cancel out.
Vertically upwards, along the central axis of the coil.
Horizontal, in the plane of the coil, circling like the current.
Vertically downwards, along the central axis of the coil.
mcqs.specStatementText: magnetic field lines.
mcqs.explain: Apply the right-hand grip rule to any part of the coil: with the thumb along the anticlockwise current, the curled fingers pass upwards through the inside of the loop. Every part gives an upward field at the centre, so the field there is vertically upwards, along the axis.
rationales: A student who thinks opposite currents give cancelling fields picks this. The centre is on opposite sides of the two currents, so the grip rule gives the same direction for both: the fields add, upwards along the axis.

Apply the right-hand grip rule to any part of the coil: with the thumb along the anticlockwise current, the curled fingers pass upwards through the inside of the loop. Every part gives an upward field at the centre, so the field there is vertically upwards, along the axis.

A student who thinks the field points along the current picks this. The field is perpendicular to the current in each part of the coil, so at the centre it is along the axis, perpendicular to the plane of the coil.

A student who uses the left hand, or curls the fingers the wrong way, gets the reversed direction. With the right thumb along the anticlockwise current, the curled fingers pass upwards through the inside of the loop: the field at the centre is upwards.

mcqs.q: A long air-core solenoid carries a steady current. Which description of its magnetic field lines is correct?
options: Almost no field inside; outside, lines loop from one end to the other, as for a bar magnet.
Strongest inside at the two ends, where the lines crowd together, and weakest at the centre.
Lines start at the north-pole end and stop at the south-pole end, so none of them form closed loops.
Parallel, evenly spaced lines inside; outside, like a bar magnet's; each is a closed loop.
mcqs.specStatementText: magnetic field lines.
mcqs.explain: Inside a long solenoid the field is strong and nearly uniform along the axis. Outside, the pattern resembles a bar magnet's. Every line is a closed loop, returning through the inside of the solenoid.
rationales: A student who knows only the outside pattern of a bar magnet picks this. The lines continue through the inside of the solenoid, where the field is strongest.
A student who thinks the field is strongest at the poles picks this. Inside a long solenoid the field is nearly uniform over most of the length and falls near the ends, where the lines spread out.
A student who treats magnetic field lines like electric ones, beginning and ending on something, picks this. There are no isolated poles: every magnetic field line is a closed loop.
Inside a long solenoid the field is strong and nearly uniform along the axis. Outside, the pattern resembles a bar magnet's. Every line is a closed loop, returning through the inside of the solenoid.

mcqs.q: Two small spheres, each carrying a positive charge, are brought from infinite separation to a separation r. Which statement about the electric potential energy E_p of the system is correct?
options: It is positive, since positive work must be done to push the like charges together.
It is negative, as it is for two masses, since E_p is zero at infinite separation.
It is stored in the sphere that was moved, not in the system of the two spheres.
It is positive, and it becomes larger if the spheres are moved further apart.
mcqs.specStatementText: the electric potential energy E_p in terms of work done to assemble the system from infinite separation
mcqs.explain: E_p is the work done to assemble the system from infinite separation, where E_p = 0. Like charges repel, so an external force must do positive work to bring them together: E_p = kq₁q₂/r > 0.
rationales: E_p is the work done to assemble the system from infinite separation, where E_p = 0. Like charges repel, so an external force must do positive work to bring them together: E_p = kq₁q₂/r > 0.
A student who carries over the result for gravity picks this. Gravitational E_p is negative because masses attract; like charges repel, so the work to assemble them, and E_p, is positive.
A student who assigns potential energy to one object picks this. E_p = kq₁q₂/r depends on both charges and their separation; it belongs to the system.
A student who carries over 'higher means more E_p' from mgh picks this. For like charges E_p = kq₁q₂/r falls as r increases: they repel, so moving apart releases energy.

mcqs.q: In a simple model of the hydrogen atom, the electron is 5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ m from the proton. Take e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹. What is the electric potential energy of the electron–proton system?
mcqs.specStatementText: the electric potential energy for a system of two charged bodies as given by E_p = k q₁q₂/r
mcqs.explain: E_p = kq₁q₂/r with k = 1/4πε₀ = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²: E_p = 8.99 × 10⁹ × (+1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹)(−1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹)/5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ = −4.3 × 10⁻¹⁸ J (about −27 eV). Negative, because the charges attract.
rationales: A student who gives each charge its own potential energy and adds the two gets twice E_p. The potential energy belongs to the pair and is the work done to assemble it once: E_p = kq₁q₂/r.
A student who writes k = 1/ε₀, leaving out the 4π, gets an answer 4π times too large. k = 1/4πε₀ = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².
E_p = kq₁q₂/r with k = 1/4πε₀ = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²: E_p = 8.99 × 10⁹ × (+1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹)(−1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹)/5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ = −4.3 × 10⁻¹⁸ J (about −27 eV). Negative, because the charges attract.
A student who uses kq₁q₂/2r, the total energy of a charge in a circular orbit, gets half of E_p. The potential energy alone is kq₁q₂/r.

mcqs.q: Four point charges are fixed at the corners of a square of side 0.20 m. Three of the charges are +2.0 nC and the fourth is −2.0 nC. Electric potential is zero at infinity. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the electric potential at the centre of the square?
mcqs.specStatementText: that the electric potential is a scalar quantity with zero defined at infinity
mcqs.explain: Each corner is a/√2 = 0.141 m from the centre. Potential is a scalar: V = kΣq/r = 8.99 × 10⁹ × (2.0 + 2.0 + 2.0 − 2.0) × 10⁻⁹/0.141 = 2.5 × 10² V.
mcqs.working: Distance from each corner to the centre r = (0.20 m)/√2 = 0.141 m. Net charge Σq = 3(+2.0 nC) + (−2.0 nC) = +4.0 nC. V = kΣq/r = (8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)(4.0 × 10⁻⁹ C)/(0.141 m) = 35.96/0.1414 = 2.5 × 10² V.
rationales: A student who adds the potentials as magnitudes, ignoring the negative charge's sign, uses 8.0 nC and gets 5.1 × 10² V. A scalar still has a sign: the −2.0 nC charge contributes a negative potential.
A student who uses the whole diagonal, 0.283 m, as the distance gets 1.3 × 10² V. The centre is half a diagonal from each corner, 0.141 m.
A student who uses kQ/r², as for field strength, gets 1.80 × 10³ (which is not in volts). Potential falls as 1/r: V = kQ/r.
Each corner is a/√2 = 0.141 m from the centre. Potential is a scalar: V = kΣq/r = 8.99 × 10⁹ × (2.0 + 2.0 + 2.0 − 2.0) × 10⁻⁹/0.141 = 2.5 × 10² V.

mcqs.q: Point P is a distance r from an isolated point charge −Q. Which statement about the electric potential at P is correct?
options: It is directed towards the charge, with a size equal to the work done per unit charge from infinity to P.
It is the work done per unit charge to bring a small positive test charge from infinity to P.
It is the potential energy, measured in joules, of any small charge that happens to be placed at P.
It is inversely proportional to r², falling off in the same way as the field strength.
mcqs.specStatementText: that the electric potential V_e at a point is the work done per unit charge to bring a test charge from infinity to that point as given by V_e = kQ/r
mcqs.explain: V_e is defined as the work done per unit charge bringing a small positive test charge from infinity (V = 0) to P. The charge is attracted towards −Q, so this work is negative: V_e = −kQ/r.
rationales: A student who treats potential as a vector picks this. Potential is a scalar: it has a sign (negative here) but no direction.
V_e is defined as the work done per unit charge bringing a small positive test charge from infinity (V = 0) to P. The charge is attracted towards −Q, so this work is negative: V_e = −kQ/r.
A student who confuses potential with potential energy picks this. V_e is energy per unit charge, in volts; a charge q at P has potential energy qV_e, which depends on q.
A student who attaches the inverse-square law to potential picks this. V_e = −kQ/r varies as 1/r; it is the field strength that varies as 1/r².

mcqs.q: In a region of uniform electric field of strength 4.0 × 10³ V m⁻¹ directed in the +x direction, point A at x = 0 has an electric potential of +500 V. What is the electric potential at point B, at x = 0.050 m?
mcqs.specStatementText: the electric field strength E as the electric potential gradient as given by E = −ΔV_e/Δr
mcqs.explain: E = −ΔV/Δx, so ΔV = −EΔx = −(4.0 × 10³)(0.050) = −200 V: potential falls along the field. V_B = 500 V − 200 V = +300 V.
rationales: E = −ΔV/Δx, so ΔV = −EΔx = −(4.0 × 10³)(0.050) = −200 V: potential falls along the field. V_B = 500 V − 200 V = +300 V.
A student who thinks the field points towards higher potential adds 200 V. The field points from high to low potential, so moving along it lowers V.

A student who takes the change in potential, ΔV = −EΔx = −200 V, as the potential at B picks this. That is only the change from A to B; the starting value must be included: V_B = 500 V − 200 V = +300 V.
A student who thinks a uniform field means a uniform potential picks this. A uniform field is a constant potential gradient: V changes by 4.0 × 10³ V for each metre along the field.

mcqs.q: Point charges +Q and −Q are fixed a short distance apart, and M is the midpoint between them. A student claims: 'The potential at M is zero, so no work is needed to bring a small test charge from infinity to M, and the test charge feels no electric force at M.' Which evaluation of the claim is correct?
options: The whole claim is right, as the field strength is zero wherever the potential is zero.
The first part is wrong, as the potentials of the two charges add as vectors at M.
The second part is wrong, as the work needed depends on the path from infinity to M.
The first two parts are right, but the field at M is not zero, as V changes with position there.
mcqs.specStatementText: the electric field strength E as the electric potential gradient as given by E = −ΔV_e/Δr
mcqs.explain: V_M = kQ/r − kQ/r = 0, and W = qΔV_e = q(0 − 0) = 0, so the first two parts are right. But E = −ΔV/Δr depends on the gradient of V, not its value: along the line V falls from +Q to −Q, so E ≠ 0 at M and a force acts.
rationales: A student who links a zero potential to a zero field picks this. E is the potential gradient; at M the potential is zero but still changing with position, so the field (towards −Q) is not zero.
A student who treats potential as a vector picks this. Potential is a scalar: +kQ/r and −kQ/r add algebraically to zero at M.
A student who thinks work depends on the route picks this. The electric force is conservative: W = qΔV_e depends only on the potentials at the ends of the path, both zero here.

V_M = kQ/r − kQ/r = 0, and W = qΔV_e = q(0 − 0) = 0, so the first two parts are right. But E = −ΔV/Δr depends on the gradient of V, not its value: along the line V falls from +Q to −Q, so E ≠ 0 at M and a force acts.

mcqs.q: An alpha particle, of charge +2e, is moved at constant speed from a point where the electric potential is +2000 V to a point where it is +500 V. What is the work done on the alpha particle by the external force that moves it?
options: +3.0 keV
−3.0 keV
−1.5 keV
+1.0 keV
mcqs.specStatementText: the work done in moving a charge q in an electric field as given by W = qΔV_e
mcqs.explain: W = qΔV_e = (2e)(500 V − 2000 V) = 2e × (−1500 V) = −3000 eV = −3.0 keV (−4.8 × 10⁻¹⁶ J). The field pushes the positive particle towards lower potential, so the external force must hold it back to keep its speed constant: its work is negative.
mcqs.working: ΔV_e = V_final − V_initial = +500 V − (+2000 V) = −1500 V. W = qΔV_e = (+2e)(−1500 V) = −3000 eV = −3.0 keV. In joules: −3000 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = −4.8 × 10⁻¹⁶ J. (The field does +3.0 keV of work on the particle; its kinetic energy is unchanged.)
rationales: A student who uses the work done by the field gets +3.0 keV. The field does −qΔV_e = +3.0 keV; the external force, acting against the field at constant speed, does +qΔV_e = −3.0 keV.

W = qΔV_e = (2e)(500 V − 2000 V) = 2e × (−1500 V) = −3000 eV = −3.0 keV (−4.8 × 10⁻¹⁶ J). The field pushes the positive particle towards lower potential, so the external force must hold it back to keep its speed constant: its work is negative.
A student who takes 1 eV per volt for any particle gets −1500 eV. The alpha particle's charge is 2e, so each volt corresponds to 2 eV: −3000 eV.
A student who uses the final potential alone, 2e × 500 V, gets +1.0 keV. Work depends on the change in potential, ΔV_e = 500 V − 2000 V = −1500 V.

mcqs.q: A point charge of +5.0 nC is fixed in place. A second charge of +2.0 nC is moved slowly from a point 0.30 m from the fixed charge to a point 0.10 m from it. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the work done on the +2.0 nC charge by the external force?
mcqs.specStatementText: the work done in moving a charge q in an electric field as given by W = qΔV_e
rationales: A student who uses the potential at the final point only, 450 V, gets 9.0 × 10⁻⁷ J. The charge starts at 150 V, not at infinity, so ΔV_e = 300 V.
A student who calculates 'potentials' with kQ/r² gets 8.0 × 10⁻⁶ J. Potential falls as 1/r, so V = kQ/r at each point.
A student who multiplies the force at the start by the 0.20 m moved gets 2.0 × 10⁻⁷ J. The force grows as the charges approach (∝ 1/r²), so W = Fd with one value of F is wrong; use W = qΔV_e.

mcqs.q: Equipotential surfaces are drawn at equal steps of potential. Which description is correct for the arrangement named?
options: Between oppositely charged parallel plates: evenly spaced planes parallel to the plates.
Around an isolated point charge: concentric spheres, evenly spaced from the charge outwards.
Inside a charged hollow metal sphere: the potential is zero everywhere, as the field is zero.
Near two equal positive point charges: curves that follow the field lines out from the charges.
mcqs.specStatementText: equipotential surfaces for electric fields
mcqs.explain: Between the plates (away from the edges) E is uniform, so V changes by equal amounts in equal distances: the equipotentials are equally spaced planes parallel to the plates, perpendicular to the field lines.
rationales: Between the plates (away from the edges) E is uniform, so V changes by equal amounts in equal distances: the equipotentials are equally spaced planes parallel to the plates, perpendicular to the field lines.

A student who carries over the parallel-plate pattern picks this. V = kQ/r changes fastest near the charge, so equal steps of V give spheres that are close together near the charge and further apart further out.

A student who links zero field to zero potential picks this. With no field inside, no work is done moving a charge inside, so the whole interior is at the same potential as the surface, kQ/R, which is not zero.
A student who confuses equipotentials with field lines picks this. Equipotentials cross the field lines at right angles; near each charge they are closed surfaces around it.

mcqs.q: A hollow metal sphere of radius 0.12 m carries a charge of +4.0 nC. Electric potential is zero at infinity. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the electric potential at the centre of the sphere?
options: Zero, as the field inside the sphere is zero
3.00 × 10² V, the same as on its surface
2.50 × 10³ V, from kQ/R² at its surface
Infinite, since r = 0 at the centre in V = kQ/r
mcqs.specStatementText: equipotential surfaces for electric fields
mcqs.explain: At the surface V = kQ/R = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 4.0 × 10⁻⁹/0.12 = 3.00 × 10² V. Inside, E = 0, so no work is done moving a charge from the surface to the centre: the whole interior is an equipotential at 3.00 × 10² V.
mcqs.working: Surface potential V = kQ/R = (8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)(4.0 × 10⁻⁹ C)/(0.12 m) = 299.7 V = 3.00 × 10² V. Inside a conductor E = 0, so ΔV = 0 between the surface and the centre: V(centre) = 3.00 × 10² V.
rationales: A student who links a zero field to a zero potential picks this. E = 0 means V does not change inside; it stays at the surface value, kQ/R, not zero.

At the surface V = kQ/R = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 4.0 × 10⁻⁹/0.12 = 3.00 × 10² V. Inside, E = 0, so no work is done moving a charge from the surface to the centre: the whole interior is an equipotential at 3.00 × 10² V.
A student who uses kQ/R², the expression for field strength, gets 2.50 × 10³ (which is in N C⁻¹, not V). Potential is kQ/R.
A student who applies the point-charge formula inside the sphere picks this. The charge is on the surface, a distance R from the centre; V = kQ/r holds only outside, and inside V is constant at kQ/R.

mcqs.q: A small positive charge is moved along an equipotential surface in the electric field of a fixed point charge. Which statement is correct?
options: The field is perpendicular to its path, so the field does no work on the charge.
There is no electric field on the surface, so no force acts on the charge at all.
The field does work on the charge, as the electric force acts on it throughout.
The field acts along the surface, in the same direction as the charge moves.
mcqs.specStatementText: the relationship between equipotential surfaces and electric field lines.
mcqs.explain: Field lines cross equipotentials at right angles, so the electric force is perpendicular to the displacement: W = Fs cos 90° = 0. Equivalently, W = qΔV_e = 0 because ΔV_e = 0 along the surface.
rationales: Field lines cross equipotentials at right angles, so the electric force is perpendicular to the displacement: W = Fs cos 90° = 0. Equivalently, W = qΔV_e = 0 because ΔV_e = 0 along the surface.
A student who thinks a constant potential means no field picks this. The field is not zero on an equipotential; it points across the surface, so a force acts, but at right angles to the motion.
A student who thinks any force on a moving object does work picks this. Work is Fs cos θ; with the force perpendicular to the motion, θ = 90° and no work is done.
A student who thinks field lines run along equipotentials picks this. Along an equipotential ΔV = 0, so the field has no component along it: the field is perpendicular to the surface.

mcqs.q: Point charges +Q and −Q are fixed a distance 2d apart. A small positively charged ball is released from rest at the midpoint between them. Which statement about the electric force on the ball at the moment of release is correct?
options: It is zero, since the ball is the same distance from the two fixed charges and so their forces on it cancel out.
It is zero, since the fixed charges add up to no net charge and so together they exert no force at all on the ball.
It is directed towards −Q, since it is pushed away from +Q and pulled towards −Q, both forces acting one way.
It is directed towards +Q, since it is pulled towards +Q and pushed away from −Q, both forces acting the same way in that direction.
mcqs.specStatementText: the direction of forces between the two types of electric charge
mcqs.explain: Like charges repel, so +Q pushes the ball away from itself, towards −Q. Unlike charges attract, so −Q pulls the ball towards itself. The two forces are equal in size and in the same direction, so the resultant is towards −Q.
rationales: Equal distances give equal sizes, but the directions are fixed by the signs. Away from +Q and towards −Q are the same direction here, so the forces add rather than cancel.
Each fixed charge exerts its own force on the ball. Net charge zero does not mean net force zero; the two forces here point the same way and add.

Like charges repel, so +Q pushes the ball away from itself, towards −Q. Unlike charges attract, so −Q pulls the ball towards itself. The two forces are equal in size and in the same direction, so the resultant is towards −Q.
The rule is the other way round. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract, so the ball is pushed away from +Q and pulled towards −Q.

mcqs.q: A polythene rod is rubbed with a dry woollen cloth and gains a charge of −8.0 nC. Which statement about the cloth after the rubbing is correct?
options: Its charge is −8.0 nC, because rubbing charges both surfaces in the same way.
Its charge is +8.0 nC, as the electrons the rod gained came from the cloth.
It is uncharged, because the friction created the charge on the rod alone.
Its charge is +8.0 nC, because protons moved from the rod to the cloth.
mcqs.specStatementText: the conservation of electric charge
mcqs.explain: Charge is conserved. The rod became negative by gaining electrons, and the only place they came from is the cloth, which is left short of the same number of electrons: +8.0 nC.
mcqs.working: Conservation of charge: total charge of rod + cloth before rubbing = 0, and rubbing only transfers electrons. Rod: −8.0 nC (gained electrons), so cloth: 0 − (−8.0 nC) = +8.0 nC (lost the same electrons).
rationales: Rubbing does not generate charge on each surface; it transfers electrons from one to the other. The total charge of rod plus cloth is still zero, so the cloth must be +8.0 nC.
Charge is conserved. The rod became negative by gaining electrons, and the only place they came from is the cloth, which is left short of the same number of electrons: +8.0 nC.
Friction creates no charge. The rod's −8.0 nC is made of electrons that existed before, on the cloth; conservation of charge requires the cloth to carry +8.0 nC.
Protons are bound in nuclei and do not move between solids. The cloth is +8.0 nC because it lost electrons to the rod, not because it gained protons.

mcqs.q: In an experiment of Millikan's type, an oil drop of weight 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁴ N is held stationary between two horizontal parallel plates 5.0 mm apart, with a potential difference of 500 V across them. The field between the plates is uniform. Take e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the charge on the drop?
mcqs.specStatementText: Millikan’s experiment as evidence for quantization of electric charge
mcqs.explain: E = V/d = 500/0.0050 = 1.0 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹. For the drop to be stationary, qE = W, so q = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁴/1.0 × 10⁵ = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. This is exactly 3 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C: a whole-number multiple of e, as quantization of charge requires.
mcqs.working: E = V/d = 500 V / (5.0 × 10⁻³ m) = 1.0 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹. Stationary drop: qE = W, so q = W/E = (4.8 × 10⁻¹⁴ N)/(1.0 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹) = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Check against quantization: q/e = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 3.0, a whole number, so the drop carries 3 excess electrons.
rationales: Using F = qV, q = W/V = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁴/500 = 9.6 × 10⁻¹⁷ C. The electric force is F = qE, and E = V/d, not V: the drop's charge is 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

E = V/d = 500/0.0050 = 1.0 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹. For the drop to be stationary, qE = W, so q = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁴/1.0 × 10⁵ = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. This is exactly 3 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C: a whole-number multiple of e, as quantization of charge requires.
Using d = 5.0 (millimetres not converted), E = 100 V m⁻¹ and q = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁶ C. Convert to metres: d = 5.0 × 10⁻³ m gives E = 1.0 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹ and q = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
Using E = Vd = 500 × 0.0050 = 2.5 V m⁻¹ gives q = 1.9 × 10⁻¹⁴ C. The field between plates is E = V/d, larger when the plates are closer, so q = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

mcqs.q: A sketch shows the electric field lines near a charged object. A small positive test charge is placed at a point P that lies midway between two neighbouring field lines, in a region where the lines are closely spaced. Which statement is correct?
options: No force acts on it at P, since the electric field exists only along the lines that are drawn.
A force acts on it at P, but its size cannot be judged, as the number of lines drawn is a matter of choice.
A force acts on it at P, of the same size as anywhere between those two lines, as the field is constant along a line.
A force acts on it at P, and the close spacing of the lines shows that the field there is relatively strong.
mcqs.specStatementText: the relationship between field line density and field strength
mcqs.explain: The field fills the whole region; the drawn lines are a sample of it. At P the force is along the local field direction, and its size is indicated by how closely the lines are spaced there.
rationales: The lines are a representation, not the field itself. Infinitely many lines could be drawn; the field, and the force on the charge, exist at P just as on a line.
The number drawn is a choice, but once chosen, the lines are spaced in proportion to the field strength. Close spacing at P means a relatively strong field there.
The field is not constant along a line. Where the two lines spread apart further along, the field between them is weaker; the local spacing gives the local strength.
The field fills the whole region; the drawn lines are a sample of it. At P the force is along the local field direction, and its size is indicated by how closely the lines are spaced there.

mcqs.q: Three point charges, each of +2.0 nC, are brought from infinite separation and fixed at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side 0.10 m. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the total work done by the external forces to assemble the system?
mcqs.specStatementText: the electric potential energy E_p in terms of work done to assemble the system from infinite separation
mcqs.explain: Bringing in the first charge needs no work. The second needs kq²/a = 3.6 × 10⁻⁷ J against the first. The third needs kq²/a against each of the two already there, 7.2 × 10⁻⁷ J. Total: 3 pairs × 3.6 × 10⁻⁷ J = 1.1 × 10⁻⁶ J.
mcqs.working: The work done to assemble the system is the electric potential energy of the system: the sum over every pair, E_p = Σ kq₁q₂/r. Three pairs, each with kq²/a = (8.99 × 10⁹)(2.0 × 10⁻⁹)²/0.10 = 3.60 × 10⁻⁷ J. Total W = 3 × 3.60 × 10⁻⁷ = 1.08 × 10⁻⁶ J ≈ 1.1 × 10⁻⁶ J (positive: work must be done to push like charges together).
rationales: Counting each pair twice (an energy 'for each charge' of the pair) doubles the answer. Each pair shares one potential energy kq₁q₂/r; there are three pairs, giving 1.1 × 10⁻⁶ J.
This is only the work done to bring in the third charge (two pairs). The energy belongs to the whole system: the second charge also needed work against the first, making three pairs in all.

Bringing in the first charge needs no work. The second needs kq²/a = 3.6 × 10⁻⁷ J against the first. The third needs kq²/a against each of the two already there, 7.2 × 10⁻⁷ J. Total: 3 pairs × 3.6 × 10⁻⁷ J = 1.1 × 10⁻⁶ J.
Using kq²/a² for each pair gives 1.1 × 10⁻⁵ J. Potential energy falls as 1/r, not 1/r²: E_p = kq₁q₂/r for each pair.

mcqs.q: Two point charges, +q and −q, are held a distance r apart, with electric potential energy zero at infinite separation. The separation is then increased to 2r. Which statement about the electric potential energy E_p of the system is correct?
options: E_p rises from −kq²/r to −kq²/2r, so an external force does positive work on it.
E_p falls from −kq²/r to −kq²/2r, because its size has been halved.
E_p changes from −kq²/r to −kq²/4r, because it obeys an inverse-square law.
E_p falls from +kq²/r to +kq²/2r, because potential energy is a positive quantity.
mcqs.specStatementText: the electric potential energy for a system of two charged bodies as given by E_p = k q₁q₂/r
mcqs.explain: E_p = kq₁q₂/r = −kq²/r at separation r and −kq²/2r at 2r. Since −kq²/2r is greater (less negative) than −kq²/r, E_p increases; the increase is supplied by positive work from the external force pulling the unlike charges apart.
mcqs.working: E_p = kq₁q₂/r with q₁ = +q, q₂ = −q: at separation r, E_p = −kq²/r; at 2r, E_p = −kq²/(2r). Change ΔE_p = −kq²/2r − (−kq²/r) = +kq²/2r > 0: E_p increases (becomes less negative). Work done by the external force = ΔE_p = +kq²/2r, positive.
rationales: E_p = kq₁q₂/r = −kq²/r at separation r and −kq²/2r at 2r. Since −kq²/2r is greater (less negative) than −kq²/r, E_p increases; the increase is supplied by positive work from the external force pulling the unlike charges apart.
Halving the size of a negative number makes it larger, not smaller: −kq²/2r > −kq²/r. E_p increases as unlike charges are separated, which is why work must be done to separate them.
The force obeys an inverse-square law; the potential energy is E_p = kq₁q₂/r, proportional to 1/r. Doubling r halves the size of E_p, giving −kq²/2r.

With zero at infinity, the potential energy of unlike charges is negative: the field does positive work as they come together, so E_p = −kq²/r at separation r. Keeping the signs of the charges in kq₁q₂/r gives this automatically.

mcqs.q: Electric potential is defined to be zero at infinity. A student instead takes the potential to be zero at the surface of a charged conducting sphere, and repeats a calculation of the work needed to move a small charge between two points P and Q outside the sphere. Which statement is correct?
options: The field strength at the surface of the sphere changes, because the field must be zero wherever the potential is zero.
The work needed is unchanged: every potential shifts by the same constant, and only V_Q − V_P matters.
The work needed changes, because the potential energy of the moved charge at P and at Q has changed.
The calculation is invalid, because the potential at the surface of a charged sphere is not zero.
mcqs.specStatementText: that the electric potential is a scalar quantity with zero defined at infinity
mcqs.explain: Moving the zero adds the same constant to the potential of every point. W = qΔV_e depends only on the difference between the potentials at Q and P, which is unaffected. The zero at infinity is a convention, not a law.
rationales: Potential and field strength are different quantities: E is the gradient of V, not its value. Adding a constant to every potential leaves every gradient, and so every field, unchanged.

Moving the zero adds the same constant to the potential of every point. W = qΔV_e depends only on the difference between the potentials at Q and P, which is unaffected. The zero at infinity is a convention, not a law.
The potential energy at each point does change, but by the same amount at P and at Q. Work depends on the change in potential energy between the two points, which is the same as before.
The potential at any point has no absolute value; only differences are measurable. Zero at infinity is the IB convention, but any other reference point gives the same fields and the same work done.

mcqs.q: A metal sphere of diameter 0.20 m carries a charge of +6.0 nC, spread uniformly over its surface. Electric potential is zero at infinity. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the electric potential at a point 0.20 m from the surface of the sphere?
mcqs.specStatementText: that the electric potential V_e at a point is the work done per unit charge to bring a test charge from infinity to that point as given by V_e = kQ/r
mcqs.explain: The distance in V_e = kQ/r is measured from the centre of the sphere: r = radius + 0.20 m = 0.10 + 0.20 = 0.30 m. V_e = (8.99 × 10⁹ × 6.0 × 10⁻⁹)/0.30 = 1.8 × 10² V.
mcqs.working: Outside the sphere the field and potential are those of a point charge at its centre. Radius = 0.10 m, so r = 0.10 + 0.20 = 0.30 m from the centre. V_e = kQ/r = (8.99 × 10⁹)(6.0 × 10⁻⁹)/0.30 = 53.94/0.30 = 179.8 V ≈ 1.8 × 10² V.
rationales: The distance in V_e = kQ/r is measured from the centre of the sphere: r = radius + 0.20 m = 0.10 + 0.20 = 0.30 m. V_e = (8.99 × 10⁹ × 6.0 × 10⁻⁹)/0.30 = 1.8 × 10² V.
Using r = 0.20 m, the distance from the surface, gives 2.7 × 10² V. Outside the sphere the charge acts as if at the centre, so r is measured from the centre: 0.30 m.
Adding the full diameter, 0.20 + 0.20 = 0.40 m, gives 1.3 × 10² V. The distance from the centre to the surface is the radius, 0.10 m, so r = 0.30 m.
Using kQ/r² with r = 0.30 m gives 6.0 × 10² V. That expression is the field strength (in V m⁻¹); potential is V_e = kQ/r.

mcqs.q: Three equipotential surfaces in an electric field are drawn at +30 V, +20 V and +10 V. A single electric field line passes through all three surfaces. Which statement about this field line is correct?
options: It crosses each surface at right angles and is directed from the +10 V surface towards the +30 V surface.
It runs along the surfaces rather than across them, as the electric field acts along an equipotential.
It crosses each surface at right angles, directed from the +30 V surface to the +10 V surface.
It is broken at each surface, since there is no electric field where the potential is constant.
mcqs.specStatementText: the relationship between equipotential surfaces and electric field lines.
mcqs.explain: Field lines are always perpendicular to equipotential surfaces (otherwise the field would have a component along the surface and V would change along it), and the field points from high to low potential, E = −ΔV_e/Δr.
mcqs.working: Along a field line the potential falls: E = −ΔV_e/Δr, so the field is directed from +30 V through +20 V to +10 V. On an equipotential surface V is constant, so E has no component along the surface; the field line therefore meets each surface at 90°.
rationales: The field points down the potential gradient, from high to low potential: from +30 V towards +10 V. A positive charge released on the +30 V surface would move towards +10 V.
Along an equipotential the potential does not change, so the field has no component along it. The field, and the field line, are perpendicular to each equipotential surface.

Field lines are always perpendicular to equipotential surfaces (otherwise the field would have a component along the surface and V would change along it), and the field points from high to low potential, E = −ΔV_e/Δr.
The potential is constant along the surface, not across it. There is a field at every point of the surface, directed perpendicular to it, so the line passes straight through.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows the electric field lines of two point charges, X and Y. Which statement about the charges is correct?
options: X is positive and Y negative, and the two charges have exactly the same size.
X is positive and Y negative, and the size of X's charge is twice that of Y's.
X and Y carry charges of the same sign, because the field lines join them together.
Y is positive and X negative, since the arrows show how a negative charge is pushed.
mcqs.specStatementText: electric field lines
mcqs.explain: Lines leave positive charges and end on negative ones, so X is positive and Y negative. The number of lines drawn to a charge is proportional to its size: ten leave X but only five end on Y, so |Q_X| = 2|Q_Y|.
rationales: The signs are right, but the line count is not arbitrary: it is drawn in proportion to the charge. Only half the lines leaving X end on Y, so Y's charge is half the size of X's.

Lines leave positive charges and end on negative ones, so X is positive and Y negative. The number of lines drawn to a charge is proportional to its size: ten leave X but only five end on Y, so |Q_X| = 2|Q_Y|.
Lines join two charges only when they have opposite signs; lines from two like charges curve away from each other. Lines leaving X and ending on Y show that X is positive and Y negative.
Field-line arrows show the direction of the force on a positive test charge. Arrows point away from X, so X is positive; they point into Y, so Y is negative.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows the electric field lines of a positively charged metal sphere and four points A, B, C and D. Which statement about the electric field strength E at these points is correct?
options: E is greatest at A and falls steadily through B, C and D, as the charge is inside the sphere.
E is zero at A and at B, and E is greater at C than at D, where the lines are wider apart.
E is zero at A and at B, and E at C equals E at D, since the same lines pass both points.
E is zero at A only, and E at B is greater than E at C, as B is nearest the surface charge.
mcqs.specStatementText: the relationship between field line density and field strength
mcqs.explain: No field lines are drawn inside the sphere: the field inside a charged conductor is zero, so E = 0 at both A and B. Outside, the lines spread apart with distance, so the line density, and E, is greater at C than at D.
rationales: The charge on a conductor sits on its surface, and there are no field lines inside: E = 0 at A and B. The field is greatest just outside the surface, at C, and falls off with distance.

No field lines are drawn inside the sphere: the field inside a charged conductor is zero, so E = 0 at both A and B. Outside, the lines spread apart with distance, so the line density, and E, is greater at C than at D.
The same lines pass C and D, but at D they are further apart. The field strength is shown by the spacing of the lines, not by which lines pass a point, so E is smaller at D.

The surface charge produces no field anywhere inside the conductor, not only at the centre: the contributions of all parts of the surface cancel at every interior point, so E = 0 at B as well as at A.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows a long straight wire viewed end-on; the cross indicates that the current is directed into the page. What is the direction of the magnetic field due to the wire at point P?
options: Towards the top of the page, along the tangent to the dashed circle at P
Directly away from the wire, along the radius of the dashed circle through P
Towards the bottom of the page, along the tangent to the dashed circle at P
Into the page, parallel to the current, and perpendicular to the dashed circles
mcqs.specStatementText: magnetic field lines.
mcqs.explain: The field lines are circles centred on the wire. Right-hand grip rule: thumb into the page (with the current), fingers curl clockwise as seen on the page. At P, to the right of the wire, clockwise means downwards.
rationales: This is the anticlockwise sense, which the grip rule gives for a current out of the page. With the thumb pointing into the page the fingers curl clockwise, so at P the field is downwards.
Magnetic field lines around a straight wire are closed circles centred on the wire, not radial lines. The field at P is tangential to the circle through P.

The field lines are circles centred on the wire. Right-hand grip rule: thumb into the page (with the current), fingers curl clockwise as seen on the page. At P, to the right of the wire, clockwise means downwards.
The magnetic field of a current is not along the current: it circles the wire in the plane perpendicular to the current. At P it lies in the page, along the tangent to the circle.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows a section through an air-core solenoid. Current flows out of the page in the wires above the axis and into the page in the wires below it. What is the direction of the magnetic field on the axis, inside the solenoid?
options: Along the axis, in the direction from the end labelled Q to the end labelled P
Out of the page above the axis and into the page below it, along the currents
Zero on the axis, because the fields of the upper and lower rows of wires cancel
Along the axis, directed from the end labelled P towards the end labelled Q
mcqs.specStatementText: magnetic field lines.
mcqs.explain: Take one turn: out of the page at the top, into the page at the bottom. Right-hand grip rule with the fingers following the current around the turn: the thumb points along the axis from P to Q. Every turn gives the same direction, so the field inside is from P towards Q.
rationales: This is the reversed sense. Curl the fingers of the right hand out of the page at the top and into the page at the bottom; the thumb then points from P towards Q.
The field is not along the current. Each turn's current circulates around the axis, and the field it produces inside the solenoid is along the axis, perpendicular to the plane of the turn.
The two rows are the two sides of the same turns. Their contributions on the axis are in the same direction, along the axis, and add to give a strong uniform field inside the solenoid.

Take one turn: out of the page at the top, into the page at the bottom. Right-hand grip rule with the fingers following the current around the turn: the thumb points along the axis from P to Q. Every turn gives the same direction, so the field inside is from P towards Q.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows two point charges, Q₁ = +4.0 nC and Q₂ = −2.0 nC, fixed on a line, and a point P on the same line. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the magnitude of the resultant electric field strength at P?
mcqs.specStatementText: the electric field strength as given by E = F/q
mcqs.explain: E₁ = kQ₁/r₁² with r₁ = 0.45 m: 1.8 × 10² N C⁻¹ away from Q₁ (rightwards). E₂ = kQ₂/r₂² with r₂ = 0.15 m: 8.0 × 10² N C⁻¹ towards Q₂ (leftwards). Opposite directions, so the resultant is 8.0 × 10² − 1.8 × 10² = 6.2 × 10² N C⁻¹, towards Q₂.
mcqs.working: Distance of P from Q₁ = 0.30 + 0.15 = 0.45 m; from Q₂ = 0.15 m. E₁ = kQ₁/r² = (8.99 × 10⁹)(4.0 × 10⁻⁹)/0.45² = 35.96/0.2025 = 177.6 N C⁻¹, directed away from Q₁ (to the right). E₂ = (8.99 × 10⁹)(2.0 × 10⁻⁹)/0.15² = 17.98/0.0225 = 799.1 N C⁻¹, directed towards Q₂ (to the left). Resultant = 799.1 − 177.6 = 621.5 N C⁻¹ ≈ 6.2 × 10² N C⁻¹, directed towards Q₂.
rationales: Adding the two magnitudes gives 9.8 × 10² N C⁻¹, but the fields at P point in opposite directions: away from the positive Q₁ and towards the negative Q₂. Subtract them.
Using kQ/r instead of kQ/r² gives 120 − 80 = 40 N C⁻¹. Field strength follows an inverse-square law: E = kQ/r².

E₁ = kQ₁/r₁² with r₁ = 0.45 m: 1.8 × 10² N C⁻¹ away from Q₁ (rightwards). E₂ = kQ₂/r₂² with r₂ = 0.15 m: 8.0 × 10² N C⁻¹ towards Q₂ (leftwards). Opposite directions, so the resultant is 8.0 × 10² − 1.8 × 10² = 6.2 × 10² N C⁻¹, towards Q₂.
Using the marked 0.30 m as the distance from Q₁ to P gives 8.0 × 10² − 4.0 × 10² = 4.0 × 10² N C⁻¹. The 0.30 m is the distance from Q₁ to Q₂; P is 0.30 + 0.15 = 0.45 m from Q₁.
